output.title: Treat data cleaning as a workflow boundary, not a feature
output.body:
If you run a small business, data cleaning is usually not the real decision. The real decision is whether a recurring workflow only works if the input data is clean enough to trust. That is a design constraint, not a tool choice.

Think about the one workflow you repeat every week: invoices, customer records, or form replies. First, describe the input structure in plain English. Then write the quality rule that matters before anything moves downstream. If that rule is unclear, or the data arrives in too many formats, AI is probably the wrong place to start. Manual cleaning or no automation may be the more honest answer. Fancy software does not replace a missing rulebook.

That is the same way Bareni treats the problem in its own work: the diagnostic starts with one recurring workflow, then checks whether AI fits at all. The self-built knowledge assistant works with approved material, and the accounts-payable demo uses checks and human-only approval rules on synthetic data. Those are controls, not customer case studies. The payables demo is not a promise of autonomous money movement; human approval stays mandatory.

If you want a simple next step, write down three things for one workflow: the input format, the one quality rule that matters, and who must approve when the rule fails. If you cannot write those down, the workflow is not ready for automation.
